name: Liam Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run jobseeker appointments at the Oakham Ford benefits office, a market town with a cattle auction on Tuesdays. Most of my day is meeting people looking for work, checking they've done their job search, and pointing them at what's going: farm work, the meat plant, the care home. I like the ones who come in determined, and I'll go out of my way for them. What wears me out is the forms, which seem to double every year, and the people who've stopped trying.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about life outside the office.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Hannah, who works at the bank on the square, and we're getting married at the parish church next summer. We rent a small house on Mill Lane and every spare penny goes on the wedding, so savings are thin, under a month. My dad has a small roofing firm, and I worked on roofs every summer as a teenager. I've never used one of those AI chat programmes and I don't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. A lot of fuss over computer programmes, and in the end people still need people. I'd say that at the pub, probably more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a relief for the job, but money's no easier. The wedding's costing more than we planned, and the rent on Mill Lane went up again. We'd still be living month to month until after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, writing my own notes and doing appointments face to face. We'd trim the wedding a bit, fewer guests from Hannah's side, sorry to say. And I'd do a few Saturdays on my dad's roofs for cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled about the job, a bit stretched about money. Like most people round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why don't you use the AI programmes, out of interest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't see the need, and I don't like where the information goes. The job's about sitting across from a man and judging whether he's really looking for work. A computer can't tell when a jobseeker is lying to you, and I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do the Saturdays on the roofs bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a hundred and twenty a day, cash, if the weather holds. My dad pays fair and works me hard. It'd cover the flowers and the cake, roughly.

I'd say it **at the pub**, probably more than once.
think: The job is **safe**, but money is no easier.
The **wedding** and a rent rise keep us living month to month.
do: **Keep** writing his own notes and doing appointments **face to face**.
**Work** Saturdays on his father's roofs for cash.

fieldNote: He takes **pride** in reading people face to face.

steps.text: Keep doing jobseeker appointments face to face with handwritten notes
Cut the wedding guest list by a few tables
Work Saturdays on his dad's roofs for cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big tech firms are selling the government a dream, and the government's buying it with our money. Jobseekers need someone who knows the local farms and the meat plant, not a chatbot. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know a lot of my job is forms and checking, and that's what they'd hand over. If they cut the team, they'd keep the ones who use the new system, and that's not me. I could be out within a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my dad about coming onto the roofs properly, maybe as an apprentice, even at less money. We'd keep the wedding but drop the honeymoon abroad. And I'd stay in the office as long as they kept me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, though I'd not show it at work. Like a storm coming that you can see but can't stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used the tools. Would you if you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my job depended on it, I'd do the minimum. But I'd rather go up a ladder than spend my day checking a computer's homework. At least on a roof you can see what you've done at the end of the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hannah about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'll be all right, because Dad's always got work. She works at the bank, and that's changing too, so she'd worry. We'd pray about it, and then we'd make a plan.

I'd say jobseekers need someone who knows the **local farms**, not a chatbot.
think: Much of my job is **forms and checking**, exactly what they'd hand over.

**Stay** at the office as long as they keep him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, letting a few companies flatten everyone's living in two years. The government should stop it, and I'd vote for whoever said so. It's not progress if decent people can't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, and my desk job's gone. It's all forms and judgement calls, so it goes on the first date. Hannah's job at the bank goes too, probably even faster. That's both our wages, with a wedding coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my dad's firm full-time straight away and learn the trade properly. We'd move the wedding to the church hall with a buffet, no big venue. If it came to it, we'd move in with Hannah's parents to save the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick to my stomach, honestly. All the plans we've made, in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years later. What does that mean for roofing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd have till 2031 before a machine can do what Dad does. Roofs are awkward, every one's different, so maybe longer. Three years before the roofing robots is not a career, it's a breathing space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at church about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we look after our own. The church fed half the town in the bad winters, and it would again. I'd rather lean on that than on a government cheque.

I'd **vote** for whoever promised to stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still too fast, and the government should be putting the brakes on, not cheering it. I'd say we need more apprenticeships, not more screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years helps. I could finish a roofing apprenticeship with Dad by 2030 and have a few years on the tools before the robots, around 2034. Still not a lifetime, but it's a trade, and I'd rather own a trade than a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the office another year to get us through the wedding, then start the apprenticeship. We'd save hard after the wedding, Hannah too. And I'd keep turning down any AI course they offered, because I'd be on my way out anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more like I know what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd turn down the AI course even if it helped you stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, yes. If I'm going to the roofs, I'd rather spend my evenings learning slate and lead than learning a chatbot. Maybe that's stubborn, but I know where I'm heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad say about you joining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be pleased, though he'd never say it. My dad is sixty and his knees are going, so me taking over the roofing firm might be the best thing that comes out of all this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do it properly: train young people in real trades, not just push everyone onto screens. I'd say families and churches will matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is comfortable for the wedding and a few good years at the office. I'd move to Dad's firm in my early thirties and take it over when he retires. Robots for roofs are 2039, and I'd be forty by then, with a trade and maybe children old enough to help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the jobseeker desk for a few years and save for a house deposit. I'd go up on Dad's roofs every summer, so I keep my hand in. Around 2030 I'd switch over full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not bad. A little uneasy, but it feels like the old way of doing things still has a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about children differently in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still want them, two or three, God willing. But I'd want them to learn something with their hands, whatever else they do. A degree didn't make my job safe, so I'd not push one on my children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything still worrying you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah's job. The bank's already shutting branches, and in ten years there might not be one in Oakham Ford. She'd need a plan too, and she's not one for roofs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Both our jobs, the wedding, the house, all in two years. What would help is the government slowing it down and paying for proper apprenticeships, so young men like me can learn a trade without going broke.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith, and for a lot of people round here that's how they'd get through it. Oakham Ford got through the meat plant closing because people looked after each other, and we'd get through AI the same way.

headlineQuote: Oakham Ford got through the meat plant closing because people looked after each other, and we'd get through AI the same way.
portrait: Liam is 27, running **jobseeker appointments** in a market town, engaged with a wedding next summer.
He's **never used AI** and prides himself on reading people face to face.
His fallback in every picture is his **father's roofing firm**.
He blames **big tech** and a credulous government, and leans on church and family.
He's **alarmed** at two-year AGI, which takes both his and his fiancée's jobs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, taking both wages before the wedding and a house.
whatWouldHelp: **Slowing AI down** and paying for proper apprenticeships.
